newsitem.title: UK: Pre-war Byelorussia lived under reign of terror.
newsitem.headline: Pre-war Byelorussia lived under reign of terror.

text.p: Byelorussia suffered terribly in the German invasion of the Soviet Union during World War Two, losing about a quarter of its people. The Jewish population was wiped out.
Yet when they invaded in 1941, the Nazis received a warm welcome from many Byelorussians like Szymon Serafinowicz who greeted them as liberators from Stalinist rule.
The Catholic Priest in the town of Mir, where Serafinowicz was a commander of the police force set up by the occupying force, held a thanksgiving mass when the Germans invaded.
A British court ruled on Friday that Serafinowicz was not mentally fit to stand trial for war crimes. He faced three specimen charges of killing Jews during World War Two.

When war broke out in 1939, the eight million population of Byelorussia (now the independent state of Belarus) was an ethnic mix of Poles, Jews and Russians with a majority of Byelorussians or White Ruthenians.

Until 1939, the state had been divided between Poland and the Soviet Union and the Soviet-ruled east was under a reign of terror. Stalinist rulers carried out mass killings during campaigns to collectivise the peasantry.
Jews, Poles and nationalist opponents of Soviet rule were routinely executed or sent to Siberia.
Hundreds of thousands of victims of Stalin's terror were later uncovered in a mass grave dating from 1938 and 1939 at Kuropaty near Minsk.
When western Byelorussia was incorporated into the Soviet Union under a Nazi-Soviet pact in 1939, the terror campaign spread.
The Soviets held a stage-managed referendum to approve the annexation. Anyone who dared to vote against it was arrested. People with links to Polish state institutions were executed.

Consequently, there were many in Byelorussia who welcomed the German occupation and the Nazis had little trouble recruiting local police forces, like the one Serafinowicz commanded in the town of Mir.
The police assisted in the Nazi programme of extermining Jews and Byelorussia's Jewish population had been wiped out by the end of the war.
The Jews had mainly occupied the vibrant towns and cities. In Mir, they had made up around half of the 6,000 population before the war.
Under German occupation they were first rounded up and forced into ghettoes and later killed or sent to death camps.

Prosecution lawyers described how on November 9, 1941, the Jews of Mir were rounded up and shot dead at three sites around the town -- the town square, an old slaughterhouse behind the local Polish school and a sandpit.
Others were killed on the streets.

In the early months of 1942, police and Nazis swept through outlying villages in convoys of horse-drawn sledges, rounding up the Jews forcing them to lie in the snow and then shooting them dead. Their bodies were left for the villagers to bury, prosecution lawyers said.
Such events were repeated all over Byelorussia.
